newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel plan to hit bumps at Bundesbank-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Waigel plan to hit bumps at Bundesbank-analysts.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves looks set to go ahead due to the desperate plight of Bonn's finances, but it probably found few fans at the central bank, analysts said.
Waigel on Thursday put pressure on the central bank to free up billions of marks in hidden reserves by revaluing gold reserves in order to help fill Bonn's gaping budget deficit.

The Bundesbank itself avoided comment on the budget issue, saying only that near-term talks would be held to discuss changes in central bank accounting methods to harmonise German laws with European laws before the start of monetary union.
Economists however said it would be hard to put a positive spin on any changes as Germany would be seen as flirting with the creative accounting methods it had abhorred until now.
"I would not say this is creative accounting but it is on the side of fudging," said Bronwyn Curtis, chief economist at Nomura in London.
Although the Bundesbank steered clear of the touchy budget issue in its statement, economists said the topic surely came up during talks and probably encountered considerable resistance.

Two key reasons the staunchly independent central bank may have been uncomfortable with Waigel's suggestions are that any revaluation of gold could be seen to prompt an unwanted expansion in money supply as well as weaken Germany's hand in keeping certain nations out of the currency union.
"I cannot imagine the Bundesbank would like this very much much, it would fire up the money printing presses," said Stefan Pelgrim, bond market analyst at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.

Unlocking these hidden reserves, valued at around 40 billion marks, would force the Bundesbank to hand over a bigger profit to the government and this would increase central bank money supply, he explained.
The inflation-fighting Bundesbank has traditionally watched money supply growth very closely as it is seen as foreshadowing future inflation rates.

Stefan Schneider, economist at Paribas in Frankfurt, added "what is probably causing the Bundesbank some pain is that any move like this would weaken Germany's hand in keeping Italy out of the currency union."
Deutsche Bank Research economist Hans-Juergen Meltzer agreed, "this definitely weakens Germany's position on Italy."

Bond markets appeared to sense Italy's position in the race to monetary union may have just improved dramatically and sent the spread between Italian and German bonds to a record low of 148 basis points.

Economists said even though the Bundesbank is Germany's central bank, it is still a business and like all good businessmen, council members surely disliked the fact that an outsider like the finance minister tries to dictate policies.

On the other hand economists also said the Bundesbank and Bonn would need to come to some sort of agreement now to prepare for the future when the Bundesbank is no longer in charge of monetary policy in Germany.
Adolf Rosenstock, economist at IBJ in Frankfurt, said the any changes would only come into effect for the 1998 fiscal year, in time for currency union scheduled to begin in 1999.
"It would not count for 1997, and details about the revaluation of assets would still have to be worked out," he said, adding this money would not count as regular income.
No matter what the outcome of Waigel's efforts, economists remain convinced that Germany will miss its 2.9 percent budget deficit target this year.

"At some point Waigel will need to backtrack and retract his statement that three means 3.0 percent and soften his line acknowledging that a 3.2 percent deficit could still qualify Germany for currency union," Paribas' Schneider said.
